0.title: Not Alone, and Not Beyond Help
0.essay:
Perhaps food has become a battle you fight every day, usually in secret. Perhaps you are watching someone you love being swallowed up by that battle, and you do not know what to do. Either way, this study is for you, and it begins with two things you need to hear: you are not alone, and there is real help.

Naming it without shame

Eating disorders include anorexia, bulimia, binge eating disorder, ARFID and a number of related problems. They affect men and women, teenagers and adults, people of every background and every body size. They are found in churches too. Having one does not mean you are vain, weak or a poor Christian. It means you are caught in something serious and painful, and you need help, as anyone would.

Please get help today

Eating disorders are not phases or fads. They can be life-threatening: they have among the highest death rates of any mental illness. Yet people do recover, and the earlier help begins, the better. So if you have not yet done so, please see a doctor this week and say plainly that you are worried about an eating disorder. Treatment usually involves a specialist team, often with a therapist and a dietitian. This study is meant to walk alongside that treatment. It never replaces it. Using medicine and therapy is no failure of faith.

If you need help now: if you or someone you love faints, has chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat or sudden confusion, or has thoughts of self-harm or suicide, do not wait. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or go to an emergency department. You can also ring a crisis line: Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, or 988 in the United States. For support with eating disorders, the charity Beat helps people in the UK, and the National Alliance for Eating Disorders helps people in the United States.

What this study will do

You will find no weights, numbers or food rules in these pages. That is deliberate: the disorder already talks about those things far too much. Instead we will look at the struggle, at the body God made, and at the Saviour who fed the hungry and ate with his friends. The unit Hard Cases: Eating Disorders: Anorexia and Bulimia in the study Biblical Counseling is written for pastors and counsellors; this study is for those who struggle and those who love them.

The chapters

More Than Food; The Lies It Tells; The Body God Made and Loves; Christ for the One Who Struggles; The Road to Recovery; and For Families and Friends.

For reflection

What would it mean for you to believe that you are not alone and not beyond help? Who is one person you could talk to honestly this week?

1.title: More Than Food
1.essay:
An eating disorder looks like a problem with food. It is about food, but it is never only about food. It reaches into how a person thinks, feels, relates to others and sees themselves, and it can quietly take over a whole life.

What eating disorders are

Eating disorders are serious illnesses in which a person’s eating, and their thoughts and feelings about food, their body and themselves, become disturbed in ways that dominate life and harm health. Doctors describe several kinds.

Anorexia is when a person eats far less than the body needs, usually with an intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted view of their own body. It is not simply wanting to be slim. Bulimia involves repeated cycles of eating large amounts while feeling out of control, followed by attempts to undo it. It is often well hidden. Binge eating disorder involves repeated episodes of eating large amounts while feeling unable to stop, followed by deep distress and shame. It is not greed or a lack of willpower. ARFID (avoidant restrictive food intake disorder) is when a person avoids or limits food not because of body image but because of fear, such as fear of choking or being sick, or strong sensitivity to taste and texture, or little interest in eating at all. It often begins in childhood and can affect growth and health.

Many people do not fit neatly into one of these, and that does not make their illness any less serious. Related struggles include an anxious obsession with eating only “healthy” or “pure” food, and exercise that has become compulsive. Eating disorders often travel with depression, anxiety, obsessive thoughts or self-harm.

How they take hold

God made us body and soul together: he “formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7). So an eating disorder rarely has one tidy cause. The body plays its part: family history, the workings of the brain, and the fact that being underfed itself changes the brain, making thoughts more rigid, anxious and fixed on food. The mind plays its part: perfectionism, all-or-nothing thinking, a harsh inner critic. Circumstances play their part: trauma, bullying, loss, a comment about someone’s body, a culture that worships appearance. And the spiritual life is involved: what we believe about our worth, our safety and our God. The study What Is Man? explores how body and soul belong together.

Often it begins with something that seems harmless, even good. Then, slowly, what felt like a choice becomes a trap.

How they hide

Eating disorders are skilled at hiding, and they often hide behind praise. Others admire the person’s discipline, their “healthy” habits, their self-control. Paul warned of rules that “have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body” (Colossians 2:23). Severity to the body can look like strength. It is often suffering.

You cannot tell by looking. People of any size can be seriously ill. Men and boys are often missed, because many still think of this as a women’s problem, and because the disorder may hide behind sport, training or an interest in fitness. In church it may hide behind the language of fasting and self-denial, or behind the reliable helper who serves at every meal but never seems to eat. Yet “the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). What others miss, he sees, and he sees it with compassion.

Not just sin, not just illness

Some Christians see eating disorders mainly as sin: vanity, gluttony or a refusal to trust God, so that repentance is the whole cure. Others see them purely as medical illnesses, about which the church can say little beyond prayer and kindness. Each sees something real: the first, that every struggle reaches down to our relationship with God; the second, that body and brain are truly involved.

This commentary’s view: An eating disorder is a serious illness of the whole person, and it must be treated medically, promptly, by people trained to treat it. It is also a struggle of the heart, in which lies are believed and good longings are bent, and so the word of God and the care of the church belong alongside treatment from the start. Much of it is suffering rather than chosen sin, and a sufferer should never be treated as a rebel. Where sin is tangled in, as it is in every human life, the answer is the same mercy we all need. The doctor and the pastor are allies, not rivals.

Safety first

Because eating disorders can damage the heart and other organs, a doctor’s check is essential, even if you feel fine. Fainting, chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, confusion or thoughts of self-harm or suicide need help now: call 999 or 112 (UK and Europe) or 911 (North America), or ring Samaritans on 116 123 or 988 in the United States.

An example

A student who had always been sporty began “getting healthy” in his first year at university. Friends at church praised his discipline. Nobody noticed that he had stopped coming to the group’s shared meals, that he was always tired and cold, that he could no longer concentrate. When a doctor, seeing him about something else, asked a few careful questions, he finally told the truth. Later he said, “The praise made it so much harder to admit.”

For reflection

Did anything in this chapter surprise you about what eating disorders are, or who they affect? Why do you think they are so easily mistaken for discipline or health? What does it mean to you that the Lord looks on the heart? If you are struggling, what is stopping you from seeing a doctor?

2.title: The Lies It Tells
2.essay:
An eating disorder does not only change what a person does. It speaks. Many who have recovered describe it as a voice that made promises and then made demands. Learning to recognise what it says, and why it sounds so convincing, is part of the road to freedom.

The lies it tells

The words vary, but the themes are strikingly common. “I am only acceptable if…” “This keeps me safe.” “I don’t deserve to eat.” “If I let go, everything will fall apart.” “No one would understand.” “I am too much.” “I am not enough.” Each sentence feels like plain fact from the inside. Each is a lie.

Jesus said, “you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:32). Freedom begins when a lie is named as a lie. That is rarely quick, because these lies have often been repeated for years. But it is possible, and it is one reason why talking honestly with a therapist, a pastor or a trusted friend matters so much.

A false saviour

Why does the disorder take such a grip? Because, for a while, it seems to work. It offers control when life feels chaotic. It offers numbing when feelings are too much. It offers a sense of achievement, of being good, of being clean. For some it becomes a way to punish themselves for a guilt they cannot name, or a way of saying “I am not all right” without having to say it.

Underneath are real and good longings: to be safe, to be accepted, to be comforted, to be clean. God made us with those longings, and he means to meet them. The disorder offers a counterfeit. It promises life and slowly takes it away. Jesus said, “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly” (John 10:10). The disorder steals friendships, joy, health, concentration, peace, and sometimes life itself.

A harsh master

A false saviour soon becomes a cruel master. What began as “just a little control” turns into rules that multiply and are never satisfied. The person who thought they were in charge finds that they are being ordered about. If you know that feeling, you are not weak or foolish. You are describing slavery, and the Bible knows a great deal about slavery and about the one who sets slaves free.

God asks through Isaiah, “Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy?” (Isaiah 55:2). The disorder demands endless labour and never satisfies. Then God invites: “Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good” (Isaiah 55:2). There is a better word and a kinder Lord.

Idols, named gently

The Bible’s word for something we look to for what only God can give is an idol. That word can sound like an accusation, and it is not meant as one here. Most people with an eating disorder did not set out to worship anything. A heart under pressure reached for something that seemed to help, and it took hold. Still, it can help to ask gently what the disorder has been asked to do. Has it been your way of being acceptable? Your safety? Your comfort? Your proof that you are good?

Common threads include control, appearance and approval, performance and escape. Other studies explore some of these roots more fully: The Fear of Man, Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation, Envy & Comparison and Shame. God shows us these things not to shame us but to free us. “Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!” (Psalm 139:23).

The soil it grows in

Many people with eating disorders have been hurt. Trauma, bullying, abuse, a home full of conflict, or a single cruel remark can all leave a person feeling unsafe in their own body. Anxiety and perfectionism often run deep. A culture of comparison, and endless images on a phone, can make every body feel like a problem. None of this makes the sufferer to blame, and none of it means the parents are to blame either. Families do not cause eating disorders by themselves, and they are usually a vital part of recovery.

If abuse is part of your story, please tell someone safe. If you are in danger now, contact the police or emergency services. Your safety comes first.

An example

A mother of three in her forties found herself eating in secret late in the evening, once the house was quiet, and then lying awake in shame, vowing never again. In counselling she began to see the pattern. It was not greed. It was the one moment in the day she let herself feel how lonely and exhausted she was, and the food numbed it. Naming that was hard. But for the first time in years she brought the loneliness itself to God, and told her husband how she really was.

Pour out your heart

“Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us” (Psalm 62:8). You do not have to tidy up your heart before you bring it. You can bring the lies, the fear and the tiredness just as they are.

For reflection

Which of the lies in this chapter sounds most familiar? What has the disorder promised you, and what has it taken? What good longing might lie underneath it? Who could you tell about what the disorder says to you?

3.title: The Body God Made and Loves
3.essay:
Many people who struggle with food feel at war with their own body. It feels like an enemy, a problem to be solved, something to hide or punish. The Bible speaks very differently about the body, and about the food God gives it.

Very good

When God made the first man and woman, he did not make souls and then reluctantly add bodies. He “formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7). The body was his idea, shaped by his own hands. And at the end of the sixth day, “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). That includes the human body, with its needs, its hunger and its limits.

The fall has touched our bodies, of course. They grow tired, ill and old. But sin did not turn the body into an enemy. It remains God’s good work, and he has not given up on it.

Knitted together

David prayed, “For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother’s womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalm 139:13–14). God did not produce a rough draft for you to correct. He made this body, your body, with care.

That may be very hard to believe when the mirror seems to shout the opposite. Do not expect to feel it at once. The disorder’s voice has been repeated for a long time, and God’s truth is often learned slowly, by returning to it again and again. It is still true on the days you cannot feel it.

A temple: dignity, not demand

“Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Sadly this verse has sometimes been used as a reason to diet harder or to feel guilty about the body. That is not what Paul meant. He was warning against sexual sin, and his point is the astonishing honour of the body. God himself lives in the believer, body included.

A temple is a place of glory, not a project to be punished into shape. And “you are not your own” is good news. You belong to the one who paid for you with his own blood. You do not belong to the disorder, and you do not have to obey it. To glorify God in your body includes caring for it, resting it and feeding it.

Food, God’s good gift

Paul warned against teachers who “require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:3), and then said, “For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer” (1 Timothy 4:4–5). Food is not a moral test. It is a gift.

Paul told a crowd in Lystra that God “did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness” (Acts 14:17). Notice the pairing: food and gladness. The psalmist praises God for “bread to strengthen man’s heart” (Psalm 104:15). The Preacher says, “Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do” (Ecclesiastes 9:7). Eating is meant to be one of the ways God shows his kindness and draws us together.

In recovery, receiving food with thanksgiving may feel impossible for a while. That is all right. It is a direction to walk in, not a test to pass today. If your team needs to plan your meals for a season, that is a kindness, not a lack of faith. A short, honest prayer before a meal, even “Lord, help me”, is real thanksgiving.

God became flesh

The clearest sign of how God values the body is that his Son took one. “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Jesus was born, grew, grew tired, and knew hunger: after fasting in the wilderness “he was hungry” (Matthew 4:2). The eternal Son did not think a human body beneath him. He wore it, and he wears it still.

The body will be raised

The Christian hope is not escape from the body but the resurrection of the body. Christ “will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body” (Philippians 3:21). “It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power” (1 Corinthians 15:43). That glory will not be about size or shape. It will be the body made whole, free from pain, fear and shame, fit to live with God for ever. The God who will raise your body cares about it now.

An example

A woman in her thirties, well into recovery, had always heard “your body is a temple” as a demand to try harder. Her pastor read the whole of 1 Corinthians 6 with her and asked who lives in a temple. She went home and wrote on a card: Dignity, not demand. She began praying a single line before meals, some days through gritted teeth. It did not change everything. But it changed the question from “Have I been good enough?” to “Will I receive this gift?”

For reflection

How have you thought about your body: as a gift, an enemy or a project? What does Genesis 1:31 say about it? How does 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 sound when read as dignity rather than demand? What would one small step towards receiving food with thanksgiving look like for you?

4.title: Christ for the One Who Struggles
4.essay:
It is striking how much of Jesus’ ministry happened around food. He fed crowds, ate with outcasts, cooked breakfast for his friends, and left his church a meal. The Saviour of the world is not uneasy at the table, and he is not uneasy with you.

He fed the hungry

When Jesus saw a great crowd in a lonely place, “he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd” (Mark 6:34). He taught them, and then he fed them, blessing five loaves and two fish. “And they all ate and were satisfied” (Mark 6:42). Another time he said, “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way” (Mark 8:2–3). He cared about their bodies, not only their souls.

When he raised a twelve-year-old girl from death, his first instruction afterwards was wonderfully ordinary: he “told them to give her something to eat” (Mark 5:43). The Lord of life cared about a child’s next meal.

He ate with people

Jesus ate so freely with sinners that his enemies called him “a glutton and a drunkard” (Luke 7:34). After his resurrection he revealed himself at a table in Emmaus: “he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them” (Luke 24:30). Then, when his frightened disciples thought he was a ghost, “he said to them, ‘Have you anything here to eat?’ They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them” (Luke 24:41–43). The risen Lord, in his glorified body, ate. Eating is not beneath glory.

“Come and have breakfast”

Peter had denied Jesus three times. Now, back on the lake, he saw the risen Lord on the shore. When they landed, “they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread” (John 21:9). Jesus did not begin with a rebuke. He said, “Come and have breakfast” (John 21:12). Then he “took the bread and gave it to them” (John 21:13). Only after the meal did he speak with Peter about his failure, and then only to restore him.

For someone who feels ashamed, that order matters. Christ prepares the fire and the food. He invites before he corrects. His table is a place of welcome, not inspection.

Elijah under the broom tree

After a great victory, the prophet Elijah ran for his life, collapsed under a tree and asked to die. God did not lecture him. He let him sleep, and then “an angel touched him and said to him, ‘Arise and eat’” (1 Kings 19:5). Elijah ate and slept again, and the angel came a second time: “Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you” (1 Kings 19:7). God fed his worn-out servant, gently and more than once, before he spoke to him about anything else.

If you, like Elijah, have felt that you would rather die, please tell someone today and get help now: call 999 or 112 (UK and Europe), 911 (North America), Samaritans on 116 123, or 988 in the United States.

The bruised reed

Matthew applies Isaiah’s words to Jesus: “a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench” (Matthew 12:20). He does not finish off what is already broken. The study Depression & the Christian has a whole chapter on this verse. Christ’s strength is patient with weakness, and he sympathises with it.

Received, not achieved

The disorder tells you that your worth must be earned and can be measured. The gospel says your worth is given, and it is beyond measuring. “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1). Paul could say, “the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). In the flesh: in this body, on ordinary days, at ordinary tables.

Your identity is not your shape, your control or your recovery score. “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). That means freedom from performance and freedom from the mirror. “For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery” (Galatians 5:1).

A meal of grace

On the night he was betrayed, Jesus “took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, ‘This is my body, which is for you’” (1 Corinthians 11:23–24). In the Lord’s Supper, Christ is truly present by his Spirit, and believers feed on him by faith. It is a meal for the weak and the hungry, not for those who have everything together. It is not a test of how well you are eating. If it feels hard, tell your pastor; you will not be the first. And it points ahead to a feast: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

An example

A woman who had struggled with bulimia since her teens dreaded communion. She felt too dirty to come. Her pastor read John 21 with her and said, “Jesus cooked breakfast for the man who had denied him. This table is for people like Peter, and like us.” The next Sunday she took the bread, hearing the words “for you”. For the first time in years, she said, her tears felt clean.

For reflection

Which picture of Jesus at a meal speaks most to you? What does God’s care for Elijah show about how he treats the exhausted? How is an identity “received, not achieved” different from the one the disorder offers? How might you come to the Lord’s Supper differently after this chapter?

5.title: The Road to Recovery
5.essay:
Recovery from an eating disorder is possible. Many people recover fully, and many more find real freedom where there was once only fear. But the road is rarely quick and almost never straight. It is a road walked with others, one step at a time, held by a Saviour who does not let go.

Treatment and teamwork

Recovery usually needs a team. A doctor checks the body and keeps it safe. A specialist eating disorder service may lead the treatment. A therapist helps untangle the thoughts and feelings underneath. A dietitian helps rebuild regular, adequate eating. Sometimes medicine helps with depression or anxiety that travels with the disorder, and sometimes a stay in hospital is needed. For children and teenagers, treatment often involves the whole family. After a long time of eating too little, the body must be brought back carefully, which is one reason this should always be done under medical care.

None of this is a failure of faith. Luke, who wrote a Gospel, was “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). God often gives help through doctors and therapists, as he gives bread through farmers. The pastor and the church walk alongside the treatment, not in place of it. When the disorder argues with your team’s plan, as it often will, trust the plan.

Slow, and not straight

Recovery often feels backwards. The behaviour may change before the thoughts do, and the feelings may change last of all. Getting better can feel worse for a while, because the disorder was numbing things that now have to be felt. Changes in your body during recovery may be very distressing. Tell your team; they understand, and they can help.

There will be good weeks and bad ones. That is normal. God’s work in you does not depend on a smooth line. “And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

Falling and rising

“For the righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Proverbs 24:16). The righteous person in that proverb falls, and falls again. What marks them out is not that they never fall, but that they get up. A slip, or even a longer relapse, is not the end of recovery. It is part of the road for many people. It is not a reason for despair, and it is certainly not a reason for God to give up on you.

When you slip, the most important thing is not to hide it. Tell your team and a trusted person early. “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23). Tomorrow’s breakfast is a fresh start, and so is the next meal after that.

Honesty with safe people

Eating disorders thrive in secret. Recovery grows in the light. “But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another” (1 John 1:7). That does not mean telling everyone. It means choosing a few safe people, those who will listen without panic, without lecturing and without gossip, and letting them really know how you are. Give them permission to ask.

What the church can do

Churches can help a great deal, often in simple ways. Be a place where no one comments on anyone’s weight, shape or plate, even with compliments. “You look well” can be heard very differently from how it was meant. Leave diet talk out of church meals and conversations, and do not call foods “naughty” or “good”. Do not press anyone in recovery to fast from food; there are other ways to set time apart for prayer. Include people in hospitality without making the food the focus. Offer practical help: lifts to appointments, a meal for a tired family, a regular coffee. Pray, and keep praying. “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).

Above all, be patient. Recovery takes time, and the church that keeps loving through setbacks shows something of the patience of Christ.

Safety on the road

Keep your medical appointments, even when you feel well. Fainting, chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, confusion, or thoughts of self-harm or suicide need help now: call 999 or 112 (UK and Europe) or 911 (North America), ring Samaritans on 116 123 or 988 in the United States, or go to an emergency department. Beat in the UK and the National Alliance for Eating Disorders in the United States offer support along the way.

An example

A young woman two years into recovery hit a hard patch during her final exams. The old thoughts came back loudly, and she started to slip. This time she did not wait. She told her therapist that week, and told a friend from church, who began texting her at lunchtime simply to ask how she was. The plan was adjusted. A few weeks later she said, “It was a stumble, not the end. I got up quicker than I ever have.”

For reflection

Who is on your team, and who might still need to be? How does Proverbs 24:16 change the way you think about a setback? Who are your safe people, and what would it look like to let them know how you really are? If you are a church member, what is one thing you could do, or stop saying, to make your church a safer place for those in recovery?

6.title: For Families and Friends
6.essay:
If you love someone with an eating disorder, you may feel frightened, helpless, guilty or angry, sometimes all on the same day. You may lie awake wondering what you missed, or what you should say. This chapter is for you. You cannot fix this alone, but you can help a great deal, and you are not alone either.

Noticing

Eating disorders are easy to miss. Signs that something may be wrong include: avoiding shared meals or eating very differently with others; secrecy around food; a growing preoccupation with food, body shape or exercise; anxiety or irritability around mealtimes; withdrawal from friends; low mood; tiredness, dizziness or always feeling cold; and, in children, not growing as expected. Changes in weight may go either way, or may not be visible at all. You do not need to be sure before you act. A concern is enough to start a conversation, and to see a doctor.

How to speak

Choose a calm, private moment, not a mealtime and not in the middle of a row. Speak about the person, not about food or weight: “I’ve noticed you seem really low, and you don’t seem yourself. I love you, and I’m worried.” Listen more than you talk. “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger” (James 1:19).

Expect denial, anger or tears. The disorder often fights being noticed. That does not mean you were wrong to speak. Stay kind, stay steady, and come back to it. “Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body” (Proverbs 16:24).

What not to say

Avoid “Just eat,” or “Why can’t you just stop?” If it were that simple, they would. Avoid comments on appearance, even kind ones: “You look healthy now” can be heard as an alarm. Avoid threats, bribes and shame. Avoid turning it into a spiritual failure: “You need to pray more” or “You have so much to be thankful for.” And do not appoint yourself the food police. If the treatment team asks you to support meals, as it often does for children and teenagers, follow their guidance closely. Otherwise, leave the food to the professionals and keep your focus on the person.

Do not blame yourself, and do not blame them. Families do not cause eating disorders by themselves, and they are usually one of the most important parts of recovery.

Getting help

For an adult, encourage them to see a doctor, and offer to go with them. For a child or teenager, act urgently. Book an appointment with the family doctor quickly and say plainly, “I am worried my child has an eating disorder.” Ask what specialist help is available. Do not wait for your child to agree that there is a problem; often they will not, and early treatment makes a real difference. You have both the authority and the responsibility to get them help.

If they faint, have chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat or confusion, or speak of self-harm or suicide, get help now: call 999 or 112 (UK and Europe) or 911 (North America), go to an emergency department, or ring Samaritans on 116 123 or 988 in the United States. Beat in the UK and the National Alliance for Eating Disorders in the United States also support families and friends.

Caring for yourself and the rest of the family

Caring for someone with an eating disorder is exhausting. Do not neglect the rest of the family: brothers and sisters can feel frightened, forgotten or resentful, and they need time and attention too. Husbands and wives need to stay on the same side. Get support for yourself, from friends, your church, your doctor, or a carers’ group. Remember Elijah: God fed and rested his servant before asking anything more of him. You need food, sleep and friends too. The Lord, Isaiah says, will “gently lead those that are with young” (Isaiah 40:11), and he leads tired parents gently.

Praying and persevering

You are not your loved one’s saviour. Christ is. That is a relief, not a defeat. You can do your part, and leave the rest with him. “Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us” (Psalm 62:8). Tell him your fears, your anger and your hopes.

In Jesus’ story, the father was watching the road: “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him” (Luke 15:20). Your loved one is not a prodigal. They are ill. But you can keep watching the road with that same love, and the God who sees from a long way off watches with you. “And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9). The study Christian Parenting has more on prodigals and difficult seasons.

An example

A father noticed that his fifteen-year-old son had stopped joining the family for dinner, was exercising far more than before and had become withdrawn. He assumed it was just a phase until his wife pointed out how tired and cold the boy always seemed. They booked the doctor the next morning, and the doctor referred him to a specialist team. The months that followed were hard, and there were many nights of prayer. But two years on, the family eats together again, and the father says, “I’m glad we didn’t wait.”

For reflection

Is there someone you are worried about? What would be a kind, calm way to begin a conversation with them? Which of the things not to say do you find hardest to avoid? Who is caring for you while you care for them? What would it mean for you to entrust your loved one to Christ, who loves them even more than you do?
